data.title: Global fashion brands shift orders from Bangladesh to India amid unrest
data.description:
Key points:
  • Zara, H&M, M&S, Celio shift Bangladesh orders, mostly to India
  • Brands divert $254 million in orders as factories shut
  • Bangladesh unrest causes over $400 million in production losses
  • Rising wages, energy shortages erode Bangladesh's cost edge
  • Temporary order shifts risk becoming long-term sourcing moves

By Ruma Paul

Global fashion retailers including Zara and H&M shifted nearly a tenth of their monthly orders from Bangladesh to other Asian manufacturing hubs in the first half of November, as labour unrest disrupted production and rising costs eroded the country's competitive edge, three factory owners said.

Between November 1 and 18, brands diverted about $254 million worth of orders from Bangladesh, with most moving to neighbouring India, the owners said, a shift that represents a major blow to a key pillar of Bangladesh's economy and could extend beyond the current unrest.

Industry leaders have said rising wages, energy shortages and political uncertainty have weakened the low-cost advantage that helped make Bangladesh the world's second apparel exporter after China, prompting global brands to diversify sourcing.

The protests have caused more than $400 million in production losses, according to the Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA), in an industry that accounts for more than 80% of Bangladesh's export earnings and nearly 40% of its manufacturing jobs.

VIETNAM, CAMBODIA AND INDONESIA ALSO BENEFIT

India has emerged as the biggest beneficiary, while buyers are also looking to Vietnam, Cambodia and Indonesia to reduce supply-chain risks and improve delivery reliability, industry leaders said.

Those pressures intensified on Wednesday when Bangladesh approved a 36% increase in the minimum wage for garment workers, the smallest rise in four decades.

The increase fell well short of workers' demands to more than double wages, triggering fresh clashes with police even as Abdur Rahman Tarafder, secretary of the Ministry of Labour and Employment, said the wage increase was "satisfactory" and that he hoped all workers would resume work from Saturday.

Industry leaders said the increase would nevertheless narrow Bangladesh's labour-cost advantage over India, although union groups argue the wages remain low by global industry standards.

Babul Akhter, a union leader and workers' representative on the government-appointed wage board, said brands should not use the unrest to justify shifting orders out of Bangladesh.

He said retailers already factor political instability and labour unrest into sourcing decisions, making such moves "hard to justify" and raising "serious doubts" whether the unrest was more than an excuse.

Factory owners, speaking on condition of anonymity because of concerns about their relationships with international buyers, said the unrest had prompted Zara, H&M, Marks & Spencer, Celio and other global brands to divert orders, with India receiving the bulk of the business.

Zara owner Inditex declined to comment on Reuters’ questions, while M&S , H&M and Celio did not respond to requests for comment.

Indian textile shares rallied after the Reuters report, with Gokaldas Exports jumping as much as 11% and Trident gaining about 5%. Other potential beneficiaries, including Welspun Living , KPR Mill and Vardhman Textiles rose around 2% each.

M. Mohiuddin Chowdhury, a director of the BGMEA, said higher wages, utility and raw-material costs were adding to pressure on manufacturers "at a time when buyers are demanding lower prices and competition from rival sourcing countries is intensifying".

MORE BUSINESS AT RISK

Factory owners said the bigger concern was that diversions of business could become permanent.

Persistent energy shortages, exacerbated by the Middle East crisis, have added to production disruptions and forced some factories to rely on more expensive alternative power sources.

But Chowdhury said that price became secondary when brands were under pressure to meet strict delivery deadlines.

India can offer buyers a delivery advantage of about a week, while Vietnam and Cambodia can cut lead times by as much as 15 days, Chowdhury said.

Rival sourcing hubs can typically complete production and delivery within 60 to 90 days, compared with about 120 days in Bangladesh, he added.

The disruptions have also created production backlogs, with manufacturers around Dhaka losing an estimated 20 to 25 production days. Some are considering overtime and costly air freight to meet delivery commitments.

Khan Monirul Alam, managing director of Alps Apparels Group, which mainly supplies European brands, said the unrest was already hitting new business.

"Since November 1, most of my buyers have stopped placing orders because of the unrest," Alam said. "They are telling us our orders have been shifted, postponed or cancelled and that they have already found alternative solutions."

Political tensions surrounding former prime minister Sheikh Hasina's possible return to Dhaka from India have added to concerns about further disruption.

Industry leaders said restoring stability and uninterrupted production would be critical to retaining international buyers. Chowdhury warned that orders shifted elsewhere during periods of instability might not return even after conditions improved.

"The challenge is restoring buyers' confidence before temporary shifts become long-term sourcing decisions," he said. "Brands have options. They will not wait for us if instability persists."

data.title: Wall Street ends higher as battered AI stocks gain in volatile week
data.description:
Wall Street's main indexes ended higher on Friday and posted weekly gains as ​investors returned from the Thanksgiving holiday and flocked to hard-hit AI-linked shares.

US stocks have swung sharply this week, with Jensen ‌Huang's return as Nvidia CEO and Anthropic's brief fall below its initial public offering price adding to volatility across the AI trade.

Investors have alternated between bargain-hunting after a steep selloff and fretting over soaring AI costs, heavy borrowing and doubts about companies' returns on investment.

"The market is so oversold that a bounce was inevitable," said ​Jamie Cox, managing partner at Harris Financial Group.

Chipmakers that investors battered this month recovered ground, with Micron and Marvell gaining 7.6% ​and 7.3% respectively. The broader chip gauge also climbed 4.7%. Nvidia, after remaining weak for most of the session, ⁠ended 0.8% higher.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 591.99 points, or 1.18%, to 50,774.94, the S&P 500 gained 114.71 points, or 1.60%, to ​7,297.49 and the Nasdaq Composite gained 543.70 points, or 2.31%, to 24,129.50.

AI beneficiaries, including data-storage firm Sandisk, surged almost 16%, while optical-products maker ​Lumentum and server maker Dell also gained sharply.

AI hyperscalers — tech companies that run large data centers — also rose, with Amazon.com, Microsoft, Meta Platforms and Oracle posting gains. Tesla surged 5%.

"There is a bounce in technology which started Monday, continued Wednesday with an intraday reversal and now continues today. So much fast money has delevered out ​of tech that this could have persistence next week as they are forced to chase back in," said Andrew Slimmon, senior portfolio manager ​at Morgan Stanley Investment Management.

WEEKLY GAINS

For the week, the S&P 500 gained 5.6%, the Nasdaq rose 6.68%, and the Dow climbed 5.46%. The S&P 500 weekly ‌gain was ⁠the index's biggest since April 2025.

The S&P 500 bank index rose 1.6%, fueled by JPMorgan Chase's almost 2% gain.

The market's gains have done little to erase November's losses. The S&P 500 and the Nasdaq are on track for their worst November since 2008, pressured by concerns over tougher AI regulation following the Democrats' US midterm election victory and expectations that monetary policy will remain restrictive.

Traders are almost fully pricing in a Federal ​Reserve interest rate hike in December ​after data this week showed ⁠the US economy grew much faster than initially estimated in the third quarter and inflation accelerated further in October.

Gold and silver miners rallied as precious-metal prices recovered from a bruising few sessions. Newmont gained 5.4%, while the Global ​X Silver Miners ETF also advanced.

Vertex Pharmaceuticals slid 5.2% after the US Food and Drug Administration extended its ​review of the ⁠company's kidney-disease drug by up to three months.

US equity markets were open for a half-day session on Friday, following Thursday's Thanksgiving holiday.

Volume on US exchanges was 10.97 billion shares.

Advancing issues outnumbered decliners by a 3.25-to-1 ratio on the NYSE. There were 55 new highs and 73 new lows on the ⁠NYSE.

On the ​Nasdaq, 3,677 stocks rose and 1,135 fell as advancing issues outnumbered decliners by a ​3.24-to-1 ratio.

The S&P 500 posted 12 new 52-week highs and no new lows, while the Nasdaq Composite recorded 53 new highs and 96 new lows.

data.title: S&P 500 Achieves Its Best Thanksgiving Rally Since 2008. What’s Next?
data.description:
The S&P 500 surged 5.6% this week, its best Thanksgiving week since the 2008 financial crisis. It also marked the index’s biggest weekly gain since April 2025.

Meanwhile, the Nasdaq rallied even harder. Still, the backdrop differs sharply from 2008, and key data now looms.

Nasdaq and S&P 500 Enjoy Thanksgiving Rally

The Nasdaq climbed 6.7% over the same stretch. Just one week earlier, the index had erased all of its 2026 gains amid heavy tech and AI selling. That swing marked one of the sharpest turnarounds of the year so far.

This rapid reversal caught many traders off guard. In fact, the Nasdaq 100 posted its largest swings since April 2025 during the week.

Earlier in the period, AI and semiconductor stocks had tumbled after several volatile sessions. Then, buyers returned aggressively and fueled a strong relief rally.

The comparison with 2008 stands out.

Back then, the only larger Thanksgiving-week gain since 1950 came after a nearly 50% crash. Moreover, stocks fell almost 25% more before bottoming in March 2009.

This time, the setup looks far healthier. The S&P 500 had slipped only about 12% from its October record before buyers stepped in. That smaller pullback points to a correction, not a crisis.

Will the Stock Market Rebound In December?

Friday’s shortened Black Friday session extended the gains. The S&P 500 Trading View about 1.6% and hit one-week highs near 7,325. It then settled around 7,297.

Trading volumes stayed light because of the holiday. Even so, the upward momentum held.

Next week, investors will focus on several key reports:

  • Non-farm payrolls and unemployment data.
  • The ISM services PMI.
  • University of Michigan consumer sentiment.

Together, these reports could show whether the economy remains strong enough to support higher stock prices.

The rebound also spread to other assets. Gold climbed above $3,600, while silver topped $43 as the tech sell-off eased.

Bitcoin trades near $59,700 and looked poised to end a seven-week losing streak. However, it continued to lag the equity rebound, as crypto sentiment stayed in extreme fear.

Analysts also warned about weekend positioning ahead of the Fed’s blackout period. Ultimately, interest rate expectations will likely shape the next move for both stocks and crypto.

data.title: First Citizens Bank Acquires United Fidelity Bank Assets From FDIC
data.description:
WASHINGTON (dpa-AFX) - First-Citizens Bank & Trust Company, the banking subsidiary of First Citizens BancShares Inc. (FCNCA), has agreed to acquire substantially all loans and certain other assets of United Fidelity Bank or UFB from the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation or FDIC. The bank will also assume most customer deposits and selected liabilities of UFB after the Indiana-based lender entered FDIC receivership.

As part of the transaction, First Citizens Bank will take over 20 former UFB branches across Indiana, Illinois, Colorado and Florida, along with two Bank of St. Croix branches in the U.S. Virgin Islands. The deal also includes UFB's subsidiaries, including real estate development and management company Pedcor Homes Corporation.

Based on UFB's September 30, 2026 balances, First Citizens Bank is expected to assume approximately $5.9 billion in assets, $4.5 billion in deposits and $3.1 billion in loans. The figures remain subject to adjustment following the transaction's closing and settlement process with the FDIC.

The acquisition was awarded to First Citizens Bank through a competitive bidding process and is structured as a whole-bank purchase.

Former UFB and Bank of St. Croix branches will begin operating as a division of First Citizens Bank starting November 28, 2026. Customers will continue to have access to their accounts without any immediate changes, while the conversion to First Citizens Bank's systems will occur at a later date.

data.title: The High Political Cost of Trump's Loyalty to Jensen Huang — WSJ
data.description:
By Aaron Zitner

President Trump is increasingly building his second-term legacy on a bet that what is good for artificial-intelligence companies is good for America. Persuading Americans that he is right is shaping up as a challenge.

Trump's extraordinary push to reinstate Jensen Huang as chief executive of Nvidia was one of several actions allying him with AI-industry leaders who are building enormous wealth. They face a backlash from voters who are worried that AI will undercut their job prospects and that politicians are giving special deals to themselves and political insiders.

That public skepticism is compounding Trump's political headwinds as Congress prepares to investigate the national-security risks of the administration's interactions with Nvidia, the chip maker that is a pillar of the AI economy. Many Republican lawmakers who have overwhelmingly supported Trump in the past are now saying they plan to press his administration and Nvidia officials on whether they skirted U.S. rules designed to prevent China from obtaining the company's most sophisticated chips, and on why Trump intervened on Huang's behalf.

"The president has done a pretty lousy job of explaining the potential benefits of this technology for the U.S. economy and national security," said Scott Lincicome, vice president of economics and trade at the libertarian Cato Institute. As a result, he said, it is harder for Trump to argue that Americans benefit from reinstalling Huang as CEO.

"Rightly or wrongly, it shows a president that cares more about billionaires than average people," Lincicome said. "People turn on the TV, and Trump is intervening on behalf of his billionaire buddy."

Because Trump hasn't persuaded Americans that they will benefit personally from AI technology, voters might see his efforts to help Nvidia as a form of self-dealing, said Douglas Heye, a Republican strategist and former congressional staff member.

"Trump hasn't put in any work to convince the American people of why this is important," he said of the advancement of AI technology. "And I don't think there's a Republican on Capitol Hill who can tell you what the administration's AI policy is in any coherent way."

The party's losses in the midterms have weakened Trump's standing, leaving Republicans feeling more free to investigate whether the president's personal interests have been intertwined with government policy. Trump owns Nvidia stock that at one point in October was worth $83 million. At Huang's urging, the president approved several deals to send Nvidia chips to China and other countries posing security concerns, and he adopted an AI policy that is friendly to the industry.

Nvidia committed $25 million to the president's White House ballroom project and gave $1 million to his second inauguration.

Davis Ingle, a White House spokesman, said that the president's stock-and-bond investments are managed by independent financial institutions. "Neither President Trump nor any member of his family has any ability to direct, influence, or provide input regarding how the portfolio is invested or when investments are bought or sold," he said.

The Nvidia board fired Huang after he admitted to two extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset, only to bring him back 11 days later at Trump's urging. Huang is scheduled to be interviewed by three House committees privately Dec. 1, then in public by the Senate Banking Committee on Dec. 3.

Conservative commentators see a significant risk to Trump in the hearings.

"This is going to get ugly fast," said Jesse Waters, a Trump ally, on his Fox News program, where he connected the GOP's midterm losses to its challenge in the coming hearings.

As a billionaire "chip king," a Republican donor and admitted adulterer, Huang "isn't the most sympathetic character for the president's party to defend," Waters said. "That's going to be a hard argument to make on TV for senators who just got their heads kicked in for data centers and the cost of living."

On his podcast this week, conservative commentator Ben Shapiro warned that the Nvidia matter mixed a set of ingredients that Democrats could make politically toxic: accusations of self-dealing, a weak national-security approach to China and public anxiety over artificial intelligence.

"What if you wrap that all up into a ball and just threw that like a bomb into the middle of the American public discourse?" he asked. "Because that's what's about to happen."

White House officials say that maintaining U.S. leadership on AI will fuel revenue growth, innovation and productivity across the economy. Stocks initially rallied on Trump's success in persuading the Nvidia board to rehire Huang, which the president has called a vote of confidence in his actions.

"We have record numbers of jobs in construction, because they're building all of the new plants," Trump said in a press conference last week, "and we're going to fight very hard for the data centers." He promised to impose "tremendous penalties" on companies that build data centers in other countries rather than the U.S.

The midterm elections turned up significant opposition to data centers and anxiety about AI. Democrats such as Sherrod Brown, the party's Senate nominee in Ohio, won election after making opposition to data centers a prominent part of their campaigns. Voters in 13 states this year sided against data centers in 53 of the 54 ballot measures decided so far, according to a tally by Ballotopedia, an election-tracking site.

A large poll of midterm voters nationally found that 57% believe AI will do more to hurt society than help it, with about 25% saying they saw more benefits than harms. Three-quarters said they would oppose construction of a new data center in their community, according to the poll, called The Voter Poll by SSRS.

On Capitol Hill last week, lawmakers offered little support for Trump's decision to intervene with Nvidia on Huang's behalf. One supportive voice came from a Trump ally outside Congress. Dan Bongino, who served for nine months as deputy FBI director in Trump's current term, said on his podcast that Nvidia was right to rehire Huang, though he knew many in his audience disagreed.

"If Jensen Huang were to leave and take his talents to another company that would benefit a foreign government, folks, we're going to be screwed," Bongino said.

Write to Aaron Zitner at aaron.zitner@wsj.com

data.title: Americans Are More Exposed to the Stock Market Than Ever Before — WSJ
data.description:
By Gunjan Banerji

Americans are piling into stocks — even in the face of a brutal AI downturn.

A torrent of money has flooded into exchange-traded and mutual funds tracking U.S. stocks, at a pace with little precedent in recent history. These funds have attracted more than $450 billion in fresh cash this year, on track for a record, according to EPFR data analyzed by Deutsche Bank.

The steady stream of investment has continued even as the AI trade unraveled over the past month, a dizzying stretch of swings impacted by everything from the U.S. midterm elections to the boardroom-and-espionage drama at Nvidia. But through it all, more than $141 billion has flowed into U.S. equity funds this month, through Nov. 18 — even as the S&P 500 dropped 3.4%.

"The selloff has been met with huge inflows into U.S. equity funds," said Parag Thatte, an equity strategist at Deutsche Bank.

This insatiable appetite during this bull market, which turned four years old in October, has left many American households more exposed to stocks — and its ups and downs — than ever before. U.S. stocks recently comprised more than 40% of U.S. households' total financial assets, a record going back to the 1950s, according to Ed Clissold, chief U.S. strategist at Ned Davis Research.

U.S. stock funds added more new money than they lost for 13 consecutive months through September, the longest streak in EPFR data going back to 2000.

These inflows include investments on autopilot that more Americans make through retirement plans such as 401(k) accounts, as well as discretionary purchases. Some investors are still "buying the dip" — stepping in when their favorite stocks take a hit.

That commitment to buying stocks means Americans' wealth is also tied to the artificial-intelligence trade. AI stocks powered the market's gains for three years, before plunging in recent weeks.

Three years of double-digit returns, and even bigger gains from AI stocks, led many everyday investors to double down. Some Gen Z Americans have ditched homeownership, diverting would-be down payments to the stock market instead. Baby boomers, who have long been advised to take chips off the table, increasingly hold more of their portfolios in stocks. Many even borrowed to amplify their exposure to stocks this year.

In the mid-1980s, when Ronald Reagan was president, fewer than 30% of households held stocks, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. By the early 2000s, more than half of them did. Recently, that figure hovered around 56%, according to the Fed's Survey of Consumer Finances.

As Americans' finances grow more intertwined with the stock market, a prolonged selloff could have far-reaching effects. With the S&P 500 down 6.7% from its October record, many investors are logging on to their retirement accounts and seeing red.

Many investors have grown accustomed to lightning-fast reversals after downturns, such as those during the 2020 market crash during the Covid-19 pandemic and after "Liberation Day" last year, when President Trump's sweeping tariffs triggered a brief rout.

This recent stretch of AI-fueled volatility has dragged on for weeks and has been marked by headspinning swings that are tough for even seasoned investors to navigate. U.S. stocks recently recorded one of their worst weeks since the March 2020 crash. Many AI-related shares have fallen more than 40% from highs. The S&P 500, a real-time barometer of wealth for many of these investors, came close to wiping out its gains for the year.

Americans who are all in on the stock market, and continue to buy during big declines, are facing one of their biggest tests yet.

Following Friday's 2.3% move higher, the tech-heavy Nasdaq composite has tumbled 13% from its record hit in early October and remains in correction territory.

Strong flows into funds have been closely correlated with a stretch of strong corporate earnings reports. If investors start to doubt corporate America's ability to keep churning out profits, they might stop buying, Deutsche Bank's Thatte said.

Many of the inflows have been concentrated in exchange-traded funds, which have drawn more than $880 billion this year, a record high, according to State Street Investment Management. Mutual funds have recorded outflows.

What these investors do could have big implications for the markets. U.S. households are the largest holders of U.S. stocks, according to Goldman Sachs. And in the coming weeks, individual investors' confidence in a rebound may be the only thing standing in the way of a major downturn.

"Following a performance bloodbath and severe derisking by hedge funds during October, the support from retail investors is essential to stabilize the AI trade in November," JPMorgan's Nikolaos Panigirtzoglou wrote in a note to clients earlier this month.

Economists at Capital Economics said recently that the selloff could quickly weigh on consumer spending. From February to April 2025, a drop in the S&P 500 rapidly led to a decline in consumption, they said. The drop came as Trump's trade war ramped up, driving fears about a recession.

"There's a feedback loop," said Ed Yardeni, founder of Yardeni Research, on the relationship between stocks and consumer spending.

Write to Gunjan Banerji at gunjan.banerji@wsj.com

data.title: CryptoStar USA shuts down its last Bitcoin miners in Utah
data.description:
CryptoStar USA switched off its remaining Bitcoin mining equipment on November 23. That ends active self-mining for a company that once had operations in both Quebec and Utah.

The final shutdown covered roughly 100 machines.

CryptoStar Corp., which trades on the TSX Venture Exchange under the ticker CSTR, describes itself as a Canadian data center operator focused on Bitcoin mining. Its US arm ran its last active miners out of leased facilities in Utah.

The November 23, 2026 shutdown hit about 100 mining units. It also took offline the cooling and networking gear those machines needed to run.

The company pointed to two pressures. Electricity got more expensive under an updated utility rate structure, and the Bitcoin price declined.

CryptoStar said the two together made its mining operations unviable.

Some systems are still on. Essential safety and security systems at the Utah sites stay operational while the company works through the transition.

The shutdown follows a long retreat. CryptoStar closed its Quebec operations in September 2024, leaving Utah as its only mining site.

As of late 2024, the company reported self-mining hashrate of 21.26 PH/s from the Utah site.

In February 2026, CryptoStar raised $634,500 through a private placement funded by insiders. The money was earmarked for operational adjustments.

Now the company wants to repurpose Utah. The plan is to host customer-owned artificial intelligence (AI) and high-performance computing (HPC) equipment.

CryptoStar says it has approximately 12 megawatts of spare capacity it could put toward that work.

On November 19, 2026, four days before the miners went quiet, CryptoStar Holdings entered a strategic partnership with a US-based AI infrastructure platform provider. The partner's name was not disclosed.

The AI hosting plan has conditions. CryptoStar needs financing, customer contracts and regulatory approvals before the new business can run.

Those approvals include land-use permissions and business licenses. Timing is also an issue: a temporary data center regulation is set to expire in March 2027.

So the company has stopped mining but has not yet started hosting.

For shareholders, the near-term picture is a company with no active mining revenue and a hosting business that depends on deals not yet signed. The undisclosed partnership shows what CryptoStar intends to do; it is not a contract with paying customers.

Watch three things from here. First, whether CryptoStar names its AI partner or signs actual hosting customers. Second, whether it secures the land-use and business licenses before the temporary data center rule expires in March 2027. Third, whether it raises fresh financing, and on what terms, given that its last raise was $634,500 from insiders.

data.title: Custom Health Engages Yorkville Ives & Co. as Capital Markets Advisor to Advance U.S. Capital Markets Strategy, and Amends YA II PN Promissory Note

Key points:
  • Custom Health has engaged Yorkville Ives & Co., LLC ("Yorkville Ives"), a U.S.-based registered broker-dealer and member FINRA and SIPC, as financial advisor to support the Company's U.S. capital markets strategy.

Kelowna, British Columbia--(Newsfile Corp. - November 27, 2026) - Custom Health Holdings Inc. ("Custom Health" or the "Company"), an AI-enabled healthcare technology company building the infrastructure for medication management at home, is pleased to announce that it has engaged Yorkville Ives as its financial advisor to provide capital markets advisory services in connection with the Company's U.S. capital markets strategy.

Shane Bishop, Chief Executive Officer of Custom Health, commented, "The United States is where Custom Health is growing fastest, and our third quarter results made that clear. Our U.S. operations generated the majority of our revenue in the quarter, led by InnovativeRx and strengthened by the addition of Spencer Health Solutions, and we see a significant opportunity ahead as we scale our AdhereNet® platform across U.S. pharmacy, provider and payor markets. Bringing Yorkville Ives on as a key advisor is a natural next step in that strategy. Exploring the U.S. capital markets and access to U.S.-based growth capital are strategically aligned with our future mandate, and we believe a U.S. market presence can broaden our investor base, enhance liquidity and bring us closer to the investors, partners and patients who drive our business. We are excited to work with the Yorkville Ives team as we execute on this next chapter of growth."

Accelerating U.S. Growth

Custom Health continues to expand its presence in the United States, which has become the Company's largest revenue-generating market. In Q3-2026, U.S. operations generated revenue of US$11.1 million, representing approximately 77% of consolidated revenue of US$14.4 million, which increased 220% year-over-year. This growth was supported by the acquisition of InnovativeRx in June 2026 and the addition of Spencer Health Solutions in September 2026, further strengthening the Company's integrated medication management platform and U.S. market presence. As Custom Health continues to scale its U.S. operations, the engagement with Yorkville Ives is intended to support the Company's broader capital markets strategy.

About the Yorkville Ives Engagement

Under the terms of an engagement agreement dated November 18, 2026, Yorkville Ives will act as the Company's non-exclusive financial advisor for an initial term of twelve (12) months. The advisory services may include advice regarding the Company's U.S. capital markets strategy; the Company's capital structure, financing needs and capital markets positioning; market conditions, timing, valuation considerations and investor positioning; and the Company's presentation to the U.S. investment community.

The engagement does not constitute a commitment by Yorkville Ives or any of its affiliates to purchase, place or underwrite any securities or to provide or arrange any financing.

Amendment of Promissory Note

The Company is also pleased to announce that it has entered into an amended and restated promissory note dated November 23, 2026 (the "Amended Note") with YA II PN, Ltd. data.title: China's premium puffer jacket push meets consumer resistance
data.description:
Key points:
  • Survey finds most popular down jackets in 401-600 yuan price range
  • Peking University 399-yuan goose-down jacket sells out online
  • Canada Goose and Moncler's China momentum highlights a split between affluent and cautious shoppers

By Sophie Yu and Casey Hall

Chinese shoppers are snapping up budget down jackets as the cold weather arrives, with products priced below 500 yuan ($69) selling briskly as consumers question the value of premium brands.

A 399-yuan down jacket filled with 90% goose down and produced for Peking University sold out online in mid-November after attracting widespread attention on Chinese social media. At Walmart-owned Sam's Club, a women's down jacket from US brand Rokka&Rolla priced at 499.9 yuan also sold out, the retailer's app showed.

The trend marks a shift towards more cost-conscious spending in a market where people have long been pushed to buy more luxurious and expensive clothing. Research firm iiMedia said the average price of a down jacket in China more than doubled over the past decade and was forecast to exceed 1,000 yuan in 2025. Yet a survey released this month found jackets priced between 401 yuan and 600 yuan were the most popular among consumers.

Bosideng , China's largest down-jacket maker, has said the average price of its core products has risen to about 1,500-2,500 yuan.

A prolonged property slump, weak wage growth and concerns over job security have made many middle-class consumers more cautious about discretionary spending, raising questions about how much extra they are willing to pay for premium outerwear.

"I think Sam's has nailed that with its down jackets," said Mark Tanner, founder and managing director of Shanghai-based consultancy China Skinny.

"Many shoppers are not hunting for the cheapest copy. They want comparable design, function or pleasure without paying a large prestige premium," he said.

The challenge is becoming increasingly apparent for brands seeking to move further upmarket. Bosideng this month launched its third collection from British designer Kim Jones, but some higher-priced items saw limited sales on its flagship store on Tmall, an upmarket online shopping platform.

A blue jacket featured in advertisements with singer, actor and brand ambassador Wang Leehom carried a price tag of about 2,278 yuan but sold just 16 units in the 30 days to November 13, according to figures displayed on the Tmall store.

Bosideng did not respond to a request for comment.

VALUE OVER PRESTIGE

The diverging fortunes suggest consumers are becoming more selective rather than simply trading down.

More than 30 million down jackets were sold during this year's Singles' Day shopping festival, according to e-commerce giant Alibaba , while Uniqlo and Bosideng ranked first and second by sales, retaining their long-held positions at the top of China's down-jacket market.

Uniqlo surpassed 100 million yuan in Tmall sales within 24 minutes of Singles' Day promotions launching on October 20, Tmall said, and the platform listed the brand's lightweight down jacket, which typically retails for around 500 yuan in China, among its top-selling products.

Demand also remains resilient at the top end. Canada Goose said Greater China revenue rose 32.5% in the quarter ended September.

"China is a very healthy region for Moncler ," Chief Corporate and Supply Officer Luciano Santel said last month, as the premium outerwear brand continued to outperform a broader luxury slowdown in the world's second-largest economy.

"Like every luxury brand, they'll need to work harder than ever to justify the premium price point," Tanner said.

The contrasting performances reflect a broader divergence in Chinese consumption. As economic uncertainty weighs on middle-class households, many consumers are trading down or demanding greater value for money, while wealthier shoppers continue spending on products they believe offer them quality, performance or status.

"I definitely won't buy another down jacket that costs more than 1,000 yuan," said Lv Jiaming, a 27-year-old factory worker in Shanghai. "To me, there isn't much difference between a jacket priced at 500 or 600 yuan and one that costs more than 1,000 yuan. You can't really feel the difference, unless it's exceptionally good."

($1 = 6.6709 Chinese yuan renminbi)

data.title: FCNR flows shore up first quarter BoP
data.description:
The Reserve Bank of India’s data on balance of payments for the first half of the year brings to the forefront the overall impact of the global environment on the Indian economy. It also vindicates the decision to get in the FCNR deposits and ECBs.

The trade deficit for this half of the year was higher by $18 billion at $176.1 billion. This was a result of the oil crisis which affected both imports and exports. As refinery products are an important component of the export basket, they normally tend to support the oil equation when the price of crude oil goes up. The war disruption and closure of Strait of Hormuz meant a couple of things. First there was more dependence on Russia for oil, which came at a premium to Brent. The discounts that were had after the Ukraine war had dried up. Second, the exports of refinery products to the Gulf region came down thus pressuring growth in exports.

Second, the increase in service exports was just $6.2 billion at $105 billion. Here, software is the major contributor and was affected mainly due to the global disturbances. This may change in the coming months post US elections.

Remittances up

Remittances, however, had increased by $10.5 billion to $77.7 billion. This is significant because it was felt that the escalation of the war could impact these remittances as the flow of labour to the Gulf area had slowed down. Also, the fact that the oil industry was in disarray could have led to lower incomes. It is possible that the western nations, which are now the major sources of remittances, have contributed to this increase, as these people typically are in higher paying jobs relative to those who work in the Gulf.

The net income from abroad also widened by $6.6 billion. All put, there has been a strain on the current account. In the past, it is the capital account which has put pressure on the balance of payments. On the capital account, first the FDI in net terms increased from $7.4 billion to $ 8.8 billion. While this is higher, ‘net FDI’ remains an issue. Outward FDI was higher by $3.4 billion at $22.1 billion. Indian companies are investing in their subsidiaries or involved in M&A activity. In a way it does show that Indian companies are progressively becoming global.

Bleak FPI scene

The FPI picture was disappointing at minus $10.4 billion. While it was negative last year too, it was worse this time. There are signs that there has been a major reversal this month, and hopefully with peace being more of a reality in the Gulf, or at least oil prices remaining stable, this could increase.

The ECBs and NRI deposits need to be looked at together this time. The FCNR scheme was a major success. It was based on the concept of leverage where loans were arranged to the NRIs to invest in these deposits which yielded a return of 6.75-7 per cent per annum. These loans have been arranged significantly from Indian players as is revealed by the ECB position.

The ECBs ‘by India’ were at an all-time high of $51.4 billion. This was only $3.4 billion for the first quarter which does correlate the outflow with the FCNR scheme. It would appear that a part of these loans would have been used for leveraging the FCNR scheme. There would also be lending made by Indian companies to other overseas companies on which information is not provided separately.

The balance of payments was finally in positive territory and stood at $66.8 billion. This was largely due to the combo of FCNR and ECBs. This has also contributed to rupee stability. The country will have to arrange for the redemptions which start after three years, making forex management a 365-day affair.

The writer is Chief Economist, Bank of Baroda.

data.title: Biotech Dealmaker: Sanofi’s $41B Insmed Buyout Anchors Holiday Week As Lilly Continues Buying Spree
data.description:
Key points:
  • Paris-based Sanofi (SNY) announced earlier this week an agreement to acquire rare disease drugmaker Insmed (INSM) for $175 per share in cash, equating to roughly $41 billion in equity value.
  • AbbVie’s acquisition of Apogee Therapeutics for approximately $10.9 billion, announced in June, was the largest pure biopharma company deal of 2026 before Sanofi-Insmed.
  • American drugmaker Eli Lilly ( LLY), known for its obesity drug franchise, agreed this week to acquire UK-based and privately held LoQus23 Therapeutics for up to $725 million in cash, continuing its purchasing frenzy.

Deal activity in biotech was selective this week but featured outsized transactions, anchored by Sanofi’s acquisition of Insmed, the largest deal in the sector for 2026, while Eli Lilly extended its buying streak.

Sanofi Agrees To Buy Insmed for $41 Billion

Paris-based Sanofi (SNY) announced earlier this week an agreement to acquire rare disease drugmaker Insmed (INSM) for $175 per share in cash, equating to roughly $41 billion in equity value. The price represented about a 46% premium to Insmed’s unaffected closing price on November 18 and roughly 17% above the prior day’s close.

The deal brings two commercial respiratory medicines under Sanofi—Brinsupri (brensocatib), the first approved therapy for non-cystic fibrosis bronchiectasis, and Arikayce—plus the late-stage candidate treprostinil palmitil inhalation powder (TPIP).

Sanofi said the transaction strengthens its immunology and rare-disease respiratory franchise as it prepares for future pressure for its blockbuster Regeneron-partnered drug Dupixent and is expected to be accretive to business earnings by the end of 2028. Closing is anticipated in the first half of 2027, subject to Insmed shareholder approval and regulatory clearances.

AbbVie’s acquisition of Apogee Therapeutics for approximately $10.9 billion, announced in June, was the largest pure biopharma company deal of 2026 before Sanofi-Insmed. Earlier this year, Sanofi completed the acquisition of Dynavax Technologies for about $2.2 billion in a bid to add the latter’s adult hepatitis B vaccine HEPLISAV-B to its portfolio and strengthen its adult immunization lineup.

Lilly Acquires Preclinical Huntington’s Developer LoQus23

American drugmaker Eli Lilly ( LLY), known for its obesity drug franchise, agreed this week to acquire UK-based and privately held LoQus23 Therapeutics for up to $725 million in cash. The amount includes an undisclosed upfront payment plus development and regulatory milestones.

LoQus23’s lead asset, LQT-23, is a preclinical drug expected to treat Huntington’s disease. The company expects to submit a clinical-trial application by year-end.

Eli Lilly has been the most active large-pharma acquirer in 2026, announcing roughly 11–12 company acquisitions with total potential value, including milestones, exceeding $25–32 billion, and spanning sectors across oncology, immunology, neuroscience, vaccines, and rare diseases as it seeks to diversify its offerings and portfolio. Earlier this month, the company announced that it would buy Calytrix Bio for up to $1.5 billion. In March, the company announced it would buy Centessa Pharmaceuticals for up to $7.8 billion.

How Did SNY And LLY Retail Traders React?

On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around SNY jumped from 'bullish' to 'extremely bullish' territory over the past 24 hours, while retail chatter rose from 'high' to 'extremely high' levels.

Meanwhile, sentiment around LLY jumped from 'bearish' to 'bullish' levels, accompanied by 'normal' message volume.

While SNY has added 10% year-to-date, LLY has added 30%.

data.title: Stocktwits Biotech Dealmaker: Sanofi’s $41B Insmed Buyout Anchors Holiday Week As Lilly Continues Buying Spree
data.description:
Key points:
  • Paris-based Sanofi (SNY) announced earlier this week an agreement to acquire rare disease drugmaker Insmed (INSM) for $175 per share in cash, equating to roughly $41 billion in equity value.
  • AbbVie’s acquisition of Apogee Therapeutics for approximately $10.9 billion, announced in June, was the largest pure biopharma company deal of 2026 before Sanofi-Insmed.
  • American drugmaker Eli Lilly ( LLY), known for its obesity drug franchise, agreed this week to acquire UK-based and privately held LoQus23 Therapeutics for up to $725 million in cash, continuing its purchasing frenzy.

Deal activity in biotech was selective this week but featured outsized transactions, anchored by Sanofi’s acquisition of Insmed, the largest deal in the sector for 2026, while Eli Lilly extended its buying streak.

Sanofi Agrees To Buy Insmed for $41 Billion

Paris-based Sanofi (SNY) announced earlier this week an agreement to acquire rare disease drugmaker Insmed (INSM) for $175 per share in cash, equating to roughly $41 billion in equity value. The price represented about a 46% premium to Insmed’s unaffected closing price on November 18 and roughly 17% above the prior day’s close.

The deal brings two commercial respiratory medicines under Sanofi—Brinsupri (brensocatib), the first approved therapy for non-cystic fibrosis bronchiectasis, and Arikayce—plus the late-stage candidate treprostinil palmitil inhalation powder (TPIP).

Sanofi said the transaction strengthens its immunology and rare-disease respiratory franchise as it prepares for future pressure for its blockbuster Regeneron-partnered drug Dupixent and is expected to be accretive to business earnings by the end of 2028. Closing is anticipated in the first half of 2027, subject to Insmed shareholder approval and regulatory clearances.

AbbVie’s acquisition of Apogee Therapeutics for approximately $10.9 billion, announced in June, was the largest pure biopharma company deal of 2026 before Sanofi-Insmed. Earlier this year, Sanofi completed the acquisition of Dynavax Technologies for about $2.2 billion in a bid to add the latter’s adult hepatitis B vaccine HEPLISAV-B to its portfolio and strengthen its adult immunization lineup.

Lilly Acquires Preclinical Huntington’s Developer LoQus23

American drugmaker Eli Lilly ( LLY), known for its obesity drug franchise, agreed this week to acquire UK-based and privately held LoQus23 Therapeutics for up to $725 million in cash. The amount includes an undisclosed upfront payment plus development and regulatory milestones.

LoQus23’s lead asset, LQT-23, is a preclinical drug expected to treat Huntington’s disease. The company expects to submit a clinical-trial application by year-end.

Eli Lilly has been the most active large-pharma acquirer in 2026, announcing roughly 11–12 company acquisitions with total potential value, including milestones, exceeding $25–32 billion, and spanning sectors across oncology, immunology, neuroscience, vaccines, and rare diseases as it seeks to diversify its offerings and portfolio. Earlier this month, the company announced that it would buy Calytrix Bio for up to $1.5 billion. In March, the company announced it would buy Centessa Pharmaceuticals for up to $7.8 billion.

How Did SNY And LLY Retail Traders React?

On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around SNY jumped from 'bullish' to 'extremely bullish' territory over the past 24 hours, while retail chatter rose from 'high' to 'extremely high' levels.

Meanwhile, sentiment around LLY jumped from 'bearish' to 'bullish' levels, accompanied by 'normal' message volume.

While SNY has added 10% year-to-date, LLY has added 30%.

data.title: Zero To Sixty: Tesla Cybercab Fleet Tops 1,000 In Texas, Lucid Starts Fully Driverless Tests And Chinese EV Maker Posts Stronger Margins
data.description:
Key points:
  • Texas Department of Motor Vehicles data now lists 1,107 Cybercabs, bringing the state’s total robotaxi vehicles to 1,841.
  • Nuro, Lucid and Uber began fully driverless public-road testing of Lucid Gravity robotaxis in Palo Alto, Mountain View, Los Altos and Sunnyvale this week. 
  • On Rivian, Seaport Research initiated coverage with a ‘Buy’ rating and $18 target, highlighting the R2’s volume potential and autonomy options and terming it its top EV pick.

The Thanksgiving holiday week was relatively quiet for EV makers, but Tesla added more Cybercabs to its Texas roster in one day this week, lifting the total above 1,000. Rival Lucid began fully driverless Gravity testing with Nuro and Uber, and U.S.-listed Chinese makers reported earnings and expansion plans.

Tesla Scales Cybercab Fleet And Dallas Service

Texas Department of Motor Vehicles data now lists 1,107 Cybercabs, bringing the state’s total robotaxi vehicles to 1,841, with roughly 60% Cybercabs and remaining Model Ys.

Cybercabs, Tesla’s dedicated robotaxi offering with two seats and no steering wheels or pedals, operate in Austin and Dallas. The company launched services in Dallas last week after months of operating it purely in Austin.

Lucid, Nuro And Uber Start Driverless Bay Area Testing

Rival Lucid Motors, meanwhile, is moving towards the robotaxi market itself. Nuro, Lucid and Uber began fully driverless public-road testing of Lucid Gravity robotaxis in Palo Alto, Mountain View, Los Altos and Sunnyvale this week. Employee rides are next, the company said.

The commercial launch, earlier aimed at late 2026, is now expected in the first quarter of 2027 in the Bay Area, with Houston later. Uber has committed to buying at least 35,000 Lucid vehicles fitted with the Nuro Driver technology for its own fleet.

Analyst Names Rivian A Top Pick

On Rivian, Seaport Research initiated coverage with a Buy rating and $18 target, highlighting the R2’s volume potential and autonomy options and terming it its top EV pick.

“Smart design choices (traditional SUV shape), RIVN’s strong software and tech leadership, expanding brand awareness and strong backlog will support meaningful delivery upside in 2027,” the firm said about the R2, as reported by EV.com.

The R2 is Rivian’s latest offering, priced lower than its other models. The company started deliveries of the vehicle in June with its higher-end variant, and hopes to add cheaper variants next year. The lowest-priced variant is expected to be priced around $45,000, close to Tesla’s bestselling Model Y. The company expects the vehicle will scale volumes and drive it towards profitability.

Chinese EV Maker Updates

Chinese EV maker Li Auto, meanwhile, reported third-quarter revenue of RMB 28.8 billion ($4.32 billion), up 5.4% year over year, on 99,964 deliveries. The company’s net loss narrowed to about RMB 310 million, gross margin recovered to 16.7 percent, and free cash flow turned positive at RMB 1.96 billion. Fourth-quarter guidance is 110,000–115,000 deliveries, compared to the 109,194 vehicles it actually delivered in Q4 2025.

At the Guangzhou Auto Show, Li Auto’s rival XPeng outlines its expansion plans outside China. The company now plans five new overseas models in 2027, and aims to more than double overseas sales next year after topping 100,000 this year, and targets international robotaxi and IRON humanoid-robot deployments later in 2027.

NIO’s more affordable Firefly brand, meanwhile, reached 100,000 cumulative deliveries about 19 months after its start and expects November volume to exceed 10,000 for the first time. Firefly, Nio and Onvo brands cumulatively.

All the stocks clocked considerable gains this week. Overall, TSLA clocked 16% gains, marking its best week since May 2025. RIVN clocked 18% gains, marking its best week since July, while LI clocked its best week since March 2024 with 18% gains, while NIO added 16% and XPEV 15%. LCID was the sole player to clock single-digit gains.

data.title: JPMorgan Plans a Private Club for Well-Heeled Clients in a 1930s Branch — WSJ
data.description:
By Ben Glickman

A block off Central Park, JPMorgan Chase is turning a 1930s three-story brick building into a new offering for its richest clients: an exclusive Upper East Side club.

JPMorgan has been renovating the mansion-like structure at the corner of Madison Avenue and East 64th Street — built as an elaborate bank branch by its predecessor, Bank of Manhattan — for more than a year to allow it to serve food and drink. Public filings show audacious plans to turn the space into something akin to a members club, complete with lounges and a dining room, kitchen and bar.

The space is likely to be used as a venue to host clients of its private bank, which provides white-glove service to its highest-end customers, people familiar with the matter said. To be a private-bank client at JPMorgan, a client needs at least $10 million in investable assets.

The exact programming for the space is still being determined, a spokesman said.

The endeavor, code-named Project Ruby, is the latest effort by JPMorgan to bolster its luxe spaces and services for wealthy clients.

The bank added to its wealth-management business locations when it acquired failed bank First Republic and upgraded many of its branches into JPMorgan-branded locations, complete with additional amenities like private offices and libraries. They are a step up from its Chase brand, which is the biggest consumer bank in the country.

JPMorgan Chase has been building airport lounges, acquired travel services to plan vacations and added new offerings for its well-to-do clients, including connecting them with vendors for anything from private jets to valuing art.

These ultrawealthy customers are at the center of a fight in the banking world in recent years. The banks earn significant fees for managing their fortunes, but are fighting to take on their entire financial lives: offering advice to their estates and to their businesses.

Surging stocks since the pandemic and explosive-artificial intelligence investments have left a large and growing pie of wealth held by the top 0.1% of Americans. Blockbuster initial public offerings of long-private companies, notably SpaceX and Anthropic, have minted millionaires overnight. A generation of baby boomers is both figuring out how to spend their wealth and how to pass it down.

Other wealth managers and credit-card companies have launched similar high-end services, and some have built clubs for clients. But an expansive private-event space would be a new arrow in JPMorgan's quiver for the ultrawealthy.

The neo-Georgian building was completed in 1933 at the height of the Great Depression as a branch for Bank of the Manhattan Trust Company, which would eventually merge into Chase and then JPMorgan. In recent years it has served as an old-fashioned Chase branch for modern-day JPMorgan Chase, complete with ATMs.

It is in an elite neighborhood, standing a few steps from a window display featuring paisley leather handbags of Italian luxury fashion house Etro; the Beretta Gallery, which prominently displays hunting jackets but none of its firearms; and De Beers diamond necklaces.

The bank expects costs for the project to be about $19 million, according to an analysis of city filings by The Wall Street Journal. Records show the bank is installing a new heating, ventilation and air conditioning system, plus an elevator and two dumbwaiters for kitchen service — all part of a near gut renovation of the historic structure.

Some details of Project Ruby were earlier reported by the lifestyle newsletter run by Carson Griffith, called "Rich People Sh — ."

Documents filed with the city show that JPMorgan's project is far from complete. Work on installing piping, drains and bathroom and kitchen fixtures appears to be ongoing, according to work permits filed earlier this month.

On a recent day, small crews were installing drywall in the building, with the entire structure draped in a tarp meant to re-create the building's facade. An open door to the site on Madison Avenue showed wires still hanging from the ceiling and dumpsters holding construction materials.

Renovating an old bank branch comes with its own complications. Last year, crews spent months disassembling the old branch's metal vault, piece by piece, said Paolo Alavian, owner of Altesi, an Italian restaurant next door.

data.title: Citigroup's $35 Billion Bookkeeping Snafu Sparks Shake-Up in Upper Ranks — WSJ
data.description:
By Alexander Saeedy, Ben Dummett and Joe Wallace

A $35 billion bookkeeping blunder in Citigroup's London hub has sparked an internal shake-up and undermined efforts by America's most error-prone big bank to repair its relationship with regulators around the world.

The bank over the summer injected approximately $3 billion into a major U.K. subsidiary after an employee revealed it had been undercounting a key measure of its balance sheet, said a spokeswoman, who described the error as an "internal capital modeling issue."

The mistake shaved $35 billion off the unit's "risk-weighted assets," which regulators use to determine how much loss-absorbing capital banks need to hold. The broker-dealer subsidiary is one of Citi's biggest and most important outside the U.S.

Citi is now scrambling to limit the damage. At least two managing directors who had oversight of financial reports to regulators are no longer in their positions as of this fall, people familiar with the matter said. The bank declined to comment on their departure.

The bank's chief risk officer, Zdenek Turek, recently moved to London from New York and is working to correct the reporting issues, some of the people said.

Tiina Lee, Citi's chief executive in the U.K., said she was stepping down in October. Some of the people said her departure was unconnected to the reporting problem, but her exit adds to the turbulence in Citi's large London operation.

The Citi spokeswoman said Turek's move to London was planned before the problem came to light and was therefore unrelated, adding that the subsidiary never fell below minimum capital levels required by regulators.

The mistake is a setback for CEO Jane Fraser's attempt to draw a line under Citi's long history of unforced errors, some of which contributed to the ouster of her predecessor. The bank is still working to fix internal controls after a slapdown by U.S. regulators in 2020. That year, Citi accidentally paid $900 million to creditors of a cosmetic company.

In 2022, a Citi trader sparked a brief crash in European stocks by entering a preposterously large number in a trading system, and in 2024, U.S. regulators fined the bank $136 million for failing to make progress on cleaning up its act.

Citi has discussed the accounting problem at its U.K.-based unit with officials from the Federal Reserve, which supervises the global parent company, people familiar with the matter said. The spokeswoman declined to comment on conversations with regulators.

The problem for Citi concerns the use of proprietary financial models to calculate "risk-weighted assets," a measure that requires banks to hold more capital against assets — such as complex derivatives — that are riskier than others, such as government bonds. Some banks are allowed to use their own models to determine how much risk they have taken and the requisite capital they should hold to protect from losses.

While the U.K. regulator had given Citi the go-ahead to use some of their own proprietary models, the bank applied them beyond the scope of that approval.

The spokeswoman said the Bank of England hadn't given the green light for a Europe-based desk to use the internal models, which deployed them nonetheless.

The models undercounted Citi's actual risk-taking by around $35 billion, or around 20% of all the reported risk-weighted assets at Citigroup's U.K. subsidiary. The U.K. unit reported it had around $150 billion in risk-weighted assets last year, according to corporate filings.

Calculating risk-weighted assets is inherently complex, so errors aren't unusual. But Citi's mistake stands out for its magnitude, according to one of the people familiar with the matter.

The problem came to light after an employee rang the alarm. The bank then "quickly commenced an internal investigation and escalated this issue to regulators," the Citi spokeswoman said.

The parent company had the funds available to send capital to London and didn't have to sell stock or borrow to do so, the spokeswoman said.

A U.K. regulatory filing shows that at the start of November, Manjira Sen-Gosain, Citigroup's chief risk officer for its U.K. unit, left her position. Her LinkedIn page has been taken down.

Sen-Gosain couldn't be reached for comment.

Banks require approval from the Bank of England, which regulates banks in the U.K., before being allowed to use their own internal models to calculate risk-weighted assets. Persuading the central bank can be arduous — particularly if the model is going to be applied to a significant part of the bank's business. Risk-weighted asset models can permit significant reductions in capital requirements.

Once they are in use, the models typically have some element of self-testing. Bank of England supervisors often keep a close eye on how they are performing to make sure banks aren't undercounting, according to people familiar with the process.

It isn't uncommon for the Bank of England to approve models for certain defined purposes. Going beyond the limits of the approval can be seen as a big problem by the regulator, though how serious depends on the size of the ultimate mistake.
